
{{< slidebreak >}}

## Mixture distributions {#sec-mixture}

:::{#def-mixture}
#### Mixture density

Let ${\p_1}, \ldots, {\p_K}$ be densities on $\reals$,
and let $w_1, \ldots, w_K$ be numbers with:

- $w_c \ge 0$ for every $c$, and
- $\sumto{c}{K} w_c = 1$.

The **mixture** of ${\p_1}, \ldots, {\p_K}$
with **mixing weights** $w_1, \ldots, w_K$ is the function [@wikipedia_mixture_distribution]:

$$
{\p_{\text{mix}}}(x) \eqdef \sumto{c}{K} w_c \, {\p_c}(x), \quad x \in \reals
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-mixture-component}
#### Mixture component

The densities ${\p_1}, \ldots, {\p_K}$ in a mixture (@def-mixture) are its **components**.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-mixture-two-stage}
#### A mixture is the density of a two-stage random variable

Let $C$ be a discrete random variable
and $X$ a continuous random variable
with [joint density-mass function](random-variables.qmd#def-joint-density-mass)

$$\p(C = c,\, X = x) = w_c \, {\p_c}(x), \quad c \in \set{1, \ldots, K},$$

with ${\p_c}$ and $w_c$ as in @def-mixture.
Then:

- $\P(C = c) = w_c$,
- for each $c$ with $w_c > 0$,
  the [conditional density](expectation.qmd#def-cond-mixed) of $X$ given $C = c$ is ${\p_c}$, and
- the mixture ${\p_{\text{mix}}}$ is a density of $X$.

:::

::: proof

By the [marginal PMF from a joint density-mass function](random-variables.qmd#cor-joint-density-mass-marginal),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\P(C = c) &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} w_c \, {\p_c}(x)\,dx \\
&= w_c,
\end{aligned}
$$

because ${\p_c}$ is a density and so integrates to 1.
Then, by the [definition of the conditional density](expectation.qmd#def-cond-mixed),

$$
\begin{aligned}
\p(X = x \mid C = c) &= w_c \, {\p_c}(x) / w_c \\
&= {\p_c}(x).
\end{aligned}
$$

For the last claim, the events $\set{C = 1}, \ldots, \set{C = K}$
are mutually exclusive, and their union is the whole sample space.
So for any interval $B$:

$$
\ba
\Pr(X \in B)
&= \sumto{c}{K} \Pr(C = c,\, X \in B)
&& \text{(additivity over the events } \set{C = c} \text{)} \\
&= \sumto{c}{K} \int_B w_c \, {\p_c}(x)\,dx
&& \text{(definition of a joint density-mass function)} \\
&= \int_B \sumto{c}{K} w_c \, {\p_c}(x)\,dx
&& \text{(a finite sum of integrals is the integral of the sum)} \\
&= \int_B {\p_{\text{mix}}}(x)\,dx
&& \text{(definition of a mixture)}
\ea
$$

And ${\p_{\text{mix}}} \ge 0$, as a sum of non-negative terms,
so ${\p_{\text{mix}}}$ is a [density](random-variables.qmd#def-pdf) of $X$.

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

@thm-mixture-two-stage describes how to generate a draw from a mixture:
first draw a component label $C$ with $\P(C = c) = w_c$,
then draw $X$ from the component density ${\p_C}$.
In applications, $C$ is often an unobserved subpopulation,
such as a disease subtype.
Mixtures of multivariate densities,
such as mixtures of [multivariate normal densities](#def-mvn)
(Gaussian mixture models),
work the same way, with $p$-variable densities in place of densities on $\reals$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-mixture-mean}
#### The mean of a mixture is the weighted mean of the component means

If $X$ has density ${\p_{\text{mix}}}$ (@def-mixture),
and each component ${\p_c}$ has a defined mean $\mean_c = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, {\p_c}(x)\,dx$,
then:

$$\E{X} = \sumto{c}{K} w_c \, \mean_c$$

:::

::: proof

The integral defining $\E{X}$ converges absolutely,
because $\int_{-\infty}^\infty \abs{x} \, {\p_{\text{mix}}}(x)\,dx = \sumto{c}{K} w_c \int_{-\infty}^\infty \abs{x} \, {\p_c}(x)\,dx$,
a finite sum of finite numbers. Then:

$$
\ba
\E{X}
&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, {\p_{\text{mix}}}(x)\,dx
&& \text{(definition of expectation)} \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \sumto{c}{K} w_c \, {\p_c}(x)\,dx
&& \text{(definition of a mixture)} \\
&= \sumto{c}{K} w_c \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \, {\p_c}(x)\,dx
&& \text{(a finite sum of integrals is the integral of the sum)} \\
&= \sumto{c}{K} w_c \, \mean_c
&& \text{(definition of } \mean_c \text{)}
\ea
$$

The first step is the [definition of expectation](expectation.qmd#def-expectation).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-mixture-posterior}
#### Which component did an observation come from?

Under the conditions of @thm-mixture-two-stage,
for each $x$ with ${\p_{\text{mix}}}(x) > 0$:

$$
\P(C = c \mid X = x) = \frac{w_c \, {\p_c}(x)}{\sumto{k}{K} w_k \, {\p_k}(x)}
$$

:::

::: proof

By @thm-mixture-two-stage, ${\p_{\text{mix}}}$ is a density of $X$.
By the [definition of the conditional PMF](expectation.qmd#def-cond-mixed)
(the case $X$ continuous, $C$ discrete):

$$
\ba
\P(C = c \mid X = x)
&= \frac{\p(C = c,\, X = x)}{\p(X = x)}
&& \text{(definition of the conditional PMF)} \\
&= \frac{w_c \, {\p_c}(x)}{\sumto{k}{K} w_k \, {\p_k}(x)}
&& \text{(substitute the joint density-mass function and } {\p_{\text{mix}}} \text{)}
\ea
$$

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

@thm-mixture-posterior has the form of [Bayes' theorem](probability-basics.qmd#thm-bayes),
with densities in place of some probabilities:
the prior probability $w_c$ of component $c$
is multiplied by the component density ${\p_c}(x)$ at the observation
and divided by the overall density ${\p_{\text{mix}}}(x)$,
which plays the role of the [law of total probability](probability-basics.qmd#thm-total-prob).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-responsibility}
#### Responsibility of a mixture component

In the setting of @thm-mixture-posterior,
the conditional probability $\P(C = c \mid X = x)$ is called,
in machine learning,
the **responsibility** of component $c$ for $x$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-mixture-gaussian}
#### A two-component normal mixture

Let ${\p_1}$ be the $\ndist{0, 1}$ density and ${\p_2}$ the $\ndist{6, 1}$ density,
with mixing weights $w_1 = 0.3$ and $w_2 = 0.7$,
and let $X$ have density ${\p_{\text{mix}}} = 0.3\,{\p_1} + 0.7\,{\p_2}$.

- **Mean.**
  By @thm-mixture-mean and the [normal means](random-variables.qmd#thm-normal-moments),

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \E{X} &= 0.3 \cd 0 + 0.7 \cd 6 \\
  &= 4.2.
  \end{aligned}
  $$

- **Density.**
  ${\p_{\text{mix}}}$ has peaks near the two component means,
  ${\p_{\text{mix}}}(0) \approx 0.120$ and ${\p_{\text{mix}}}(6) \approx 0.279$,
  with a trough between them, ${\p_{\text{mix}}}(3) \approx 0.004$.
  The density at the mean, ${\p_{\text{mix}}}(4.2) \approx 0.055$,
  is less than half its value at either peak.
- **Responsibilities.**
  By @thm-mixture-posterior,
  at $x = 3$, halfway between the component means,
  ${\p_1}(3) = {\p_2}(3)$ by the symmetry of the normal density, so:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \P(C = 2 \mid X = 3)
  &= \frac{0.7\,{\p_2}(3)}{0.3\,{\p_1}(3) + 0.7\,{\p_2}(3)} \\
  &= \frac{0.7}{0.3 + 0.7} \\
  &= 0.7,
  \end{aligned}
  $$

  the prior weight: an observation equally far from both components
  carries no information about which component it came from.
  At $x = 4.2$, the same formula gives $\P(C = 2 \mid X = 4.2) \approx 0.9997$.

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

@exm-mixture-gaussian shows that the mean of a mixture
can fall where observations are rare,
so a single normal distribution fitted to such data
would describe them poorly.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-nb-mixture}
#### The negative binomial as a continuous mixture

The [negative binomial distribution](#def-nb)
is a mixture of Poisson distributions
with a continuum of components, one for each mean $\rate > 0$:
its PMF is $\P(Y = y) = \int_0^\infty g(\rate)\,\frac{\rate^y e^{-\rate}}{y!}\,d\rate$,
where the gamma density $g$ plays the role of the mixing weights
and the integral replaces the sum in @def-mixture
(see the proof of @thm-nb).

:::
